what: 0.3.0 allow-list: every difference a comparison may show WITHOUT failing, with the stage it applies from, the reference it is measured against, and the exact comparator scope. Anything not listed is a failure. THE ONE MAINTAINED LIST: the older copies in our planning notes (a short list in the plan, a list in the study notes, a row of the study's test matrix) are superseded and must not be edited. docs/ALLOWLIST.md is this file in plain words for B Jam's review; tests/check_tree.py rule 6 fails when the two name different ids. Stages are the steps of the 0.3.0 work (docs/STAGE1_PLAN.md): 0 = the 0.2.6 firmware moved into this tree; 1 = the new firmware's own start-up, scheduler, dispatcher and board layer (the FW_S1 builds: 'the stage-1 images'); 2 = the sprite engine; 3 = the unpackers, saves, zoom and MegaWire; 4 = the sound bank cache; 5 = the music, our own song engine and synth (the FW_S5 builds s5test / s5release: 'the stage-5 images'). The firmware builds B Jam tested on his own hardware are named test build 4, test build 5 (the first with our own song engine) and the stage-2 and stage-3 test builds S2, S3a, S3b and S3c. D-numbers (D01-D49) are the differences our firmware audit lists (a study of 0.2.6 against the cart's chip, not in this tree); G-, L- and U-numbers are items of our planning notes, Q1-Q7 B Jam's numbered questions. RAMDP = the cart RAM both the 68000 and the cart chip see; BRAM = the battery save RAM; VDP = the console's video chip; SAT = its sprite table; DT = Datenmeister, the music mode with the cart's own DAC; YM = the console's YM2612. scope.fpgaio: DEC_BASE (FPGAIO register 17) written by the board before each START with an entry (checked by rule, allowed transform T4 of docs/CART_FPGA_SPEC.md section 15.1; the board oracle's tag S1_LOG_DECB); the RTL's own GO at its run's end; SPTR loaded by the RTL at the START; an empty START (a load-less AF / B1) leaves SPTR where it was, where 0.2.6 rewound it to the scratch (no window read follows: counted, carried until the pointers meet again)
scope.timing: the decode runs behind the reply: AF / B1 / F2 / DA06 / DA07 finish at once, as the chip's do; the game reads the words with its VBlank DMA (AF / B1 / F2) or after busy (DA)

entries.rule: The cart's chip lists the blocks in its FPGA's queue ($1FF4 / $1FF6, $1FF2 = 0x8000) and never waits for the decode; its FPGA decodes before the game's DMA reads the window. Ours does the same with the same writes (compared write for write with the chip); our FPGA decodes into the SDRAM workspace, where 0.2.6 put the same bytes, so the window serves the same words (where the cart keeps its own buffer is not known). Compare the bytes the 68000 reads through the window; the window must never serve a word before its block is decoded (the board model's LATE count, fuzz_s1 DEC; on hardware the TEST debug save's DEC_LATECNT).

entries.name: Stage 5: synth blocks are atomic (decision 3b)
entries.against: chip (the cart-engine runner is atomic too)

scope.audio: the 160 samples (3.33 ms) of a block during which a mailbox post arrives: on the cart the post's effect can begin inside that block; on ours, as in the runner, from the next block

entries.rule: The chip's mailbox interrupt (EXTI15_10, priority 1) can preempt its mixer (TIM6, priority 3) in the middle of a block, so a post can change a voice or a channel part-way through it. The cart-engine runner (zero-time posts) and our synth mix every block whole, after every post that arrived before the block's instant (the hold-off, MCU interface v1.3 3.10.5). The synth comparisons compare against the runner strictly (0 differences); against a cart capture the difference stays inside the block a post lands in. The chip's after-mix re-check of a channel's start serial (R+0x16) therefore always passes on ours. Test build 5 (items 4 and 5 of its possible differences): the main-loop pass and its Boom Box feed ($1B90) run whole between two blocks. Measured equal to the chip for every count 0..$35 (stage 2's unit lockstep: the aging at every count and all 2,916 EC pairs). entries.name: The MegaWire's network text, not built yet: the request line, the HTTP request and its length

scope.mw_drv_bytes: DRV+0x10B6-0x10D9 (36 B: the request line 0x08020EFC writes around the server name at the MegaWire init); the HTTP request 0x08020F8C writes for a game packet in task state 3 step 1 (0x08021AC6) and for the MegaWire menu's sign-in message in task state 6 step 0 (0x08021EBC; the same buffer and length word): L bytes from DRV+0x865, where L is the chip's own 16-bit length word, L = 167 + 2n for an n-byte packet (n = 1-251, so 169-669 B, never past DRV+0xB01), plus the tail an earlier, longer request left in that buffer (the chip does not clear it between requests: at most DRV+0x865-0xB01); and that length word itself, DRV+0x107A-0x107B (2 B). Measured (mw_oracle.py's length sweep, the cart-engine runner): types 0x00 / 0x01 / 0x21 / 0x22 / 0x24 / 0x25 / 0x27 / 0x28 / 0x3F at n = 1-251, L = 167 + 2n every time; a 669-B request then a 247-B one with no re-init leaves 421 B of tail. The game's attract-mode packet (13 B) gives 193 B

entries.rule: The oracle masks only these bytes and counts every step on which they differ, with the byte extent (mw_oracle.py prints it): the request's mask follows the chip's own length word (the largest L since the chip's request buffer DRV+0x865-0x1064 was last all zero), so every chip byte past it is compared. The mask is one-sided: the port writes no byte in these ranges (it builds no network text), and a byte it wrote there is a difference; two planted controls check both edges (run_all: --plan sweep --plant 1 / 2). They are read only by the module's AT stack, which is not built (it needs a module), so no word the 68000 reads depends on them. The text is the cart's own: it is never typed into the tree (no game bytes ship); when the module path is built it is read from the player's ROM at run time and this row leaves (B51 then covers the name's bytes in it).

entries.name: The MegaWire driver's two reply-buffer pointers hold offsets into our MegaWire RAM, not the chip's addresses
entries.rule: The chip keeps two pointers into its reply buffer there (its own STM32 addresses, e.g. DRV+0x65 = 0x20010111); ours keep the same object's offset into mw_ram (MW_PTR_OF / MW_PTR, core/mw/mw.h), 32 bits on every target, the host harness included. entries.name: the anims-per-object read for an objID of 268 or more gives 0 (the chip reads its live RAM there); objIDs 256-267 as the chip

scope.commands: AD ($AD, index 0..$3F) on a record with no restart pending (+$A = 0), a queued anim (nextAnim not 0 and not $FFFF) and an objID of 256 or more: the queue's anims check (0x080194EC-0x08019522)
scope.record_words: the record's anim (+0) after such an AD, the handle's queued frame and what is drawn from it

entries.rule: The chip's AD checks a queued anim against the object's anims count, the byte at H+$404 + objID (0x2000FF20: the 256-byte table C6's anim set-up fills), with the record's whole objID. For an objID of 256 or more that byte is the chip's own live RAM after the table (H+$504 the block directory's long, the load count, then up to 64 KB of other working RAM); when it is larger than the queued anim the chip takes the queue (record anim := the queued anim, the queued frame read at the objID's directory long), else it cancels. Until stage 3 ours (core/sprite spr_frame.c spr_frames) read 0 there and always cancelled (the record's anim unchanged, nextAnim := 0, no queued frame); what stage 3 does is below. The bytes are live RAM, not ROM bytes, so the player's ROM cannot supply them (the same kind as B48). The restart path masks the objID to 14 bits and refuses one at or past the object count before any table read; objIDs 241..255 read 0 on both sides (the table's bytes there are 0). Measured (the chip's AD in the emulator, its state after C6, every objID 256..$FFFF with nextAnim 1): it read past its table for all 65,280 and took the queue for 1,341 (it depends on what the RAM holds at that moment); with nextAnim 0 or $FFFF it reads no table byte, as ours. Unreachable in play: the game has 241 objects (0..240, the anim container's count), and at every one of the 1,148,167 ADs the cart chip ran in the chip lockstep's corpora (solo, duo and attract whole, stage 04 x 3, the synthetic list with the AF unit and the tail, first boot, 3-player Arcade; RELEASE and TEST), its record's objID was 256 or more 2,352 times, every time with bit 15 and the restart flag +$A set together (the restart path, which masks it first), and the queue check read the table past its end 0 times (2,914 queue checks inside the table, 21,274 $FFFF cancels). STAGE 3 (test build S3a; B Jam's decision of 2026-10-28: do what the chip does): core/sprite spr_frame.c spr_frames gives the chip's bytes for objIDs 256-267 from ours' own state, which spr.h keeps right after frames[] in the chip's order: H+$504 the directory as the chip's 16-bit flash view address (0x6C000000 + the ROM offset, 0x080196EA), H+$508 the directory long (0x080196EE), 0x20010028 the load count, 0x2001002A-2B (no writer: 0). From objID 268 on the chip reads other live state (0x2001002C, a byte its audio init and module start clear and its audio code keeps, then the rest of its RAM), which ours does not hold in the chip's layout: ours reads 0 there and never reads past its own state. Measured (stage 3, the unit lockstep on the chip's post-C6 state, objIDs 256..65535 x 8 queued anims, 515,910 ADs): 514,546 equal, 1,364 differ, all at objID 268 or above (the chip takes the queue there when its live byte is above the queued anim); 0 of the 96 cases at 256-267 differ (stage 2's engine: 32 did). Still unreachable in play.

entries.name: an unpack job on a 0x82 stream: the chip swaps a count of bytes left over in a register; ours writes nothing

scope.commands: DA02 / DA07 (job type 3) on a stream whose type byte is 0x82 (the DA gate takes 0x80-0x82); the F4 gate takes 0x80 / 0x81 only
scope.sdram: the workspace at the DA's destination after the job

entries.rule: The chip's job step calls its 0x82 routine (0x080251C0) with a length of 0, so it writes nothing, and keeps no length: its type-3 tail (0x0801A49C) then swaps the halfwords of as many bytes as the register r7 holds, which is the last decode's length or 0, plus one for every main-loop pass since (0x0801A3B0). Ours writes nothing and swaps nothing (stage 3, test build S3a: interim/s1/bodies_s1.c s5_unpack). Measured (2026-10-28): no stream the game names is 0x82 - every DA / F4 source of the four rig corpora (526 DA02, 168 DA07, 29 F4), the 53 BGM entries, the three set-up containers and the 12,326 sprite blocks are 0x80 / 0x81; so this path is not reached in play. The chip's count depends on its main loop's pass count, which ours (a different scheduler) does not have.

entries.name: an F4 whose stream decodes past the cart chip's zoom block: the chip writes on into its own working RAM; ours stops at the block's end

scope.commands: F4 ($F4, the argument flag set) on a 0x80 / 0x81 stream (the gate takes both) that decodes to more than 4 KB: the F4 source and the save (core/zoom zoom_ss), the chip's 0x200119EC-0x200129EB
scope.chip_ram: what the chip's decode writes past 0x200129EB (its sprite engine's working RAM)

entries.rule: The chip's F4 job (type 4) decodes the stream into its F4 source at 0x200119EC with no bound, so a stream longer than the 4 KB to its zoom block's end goes on over its own live RAM (its sprite engine's, then the rest). Inside the block ours writes the chip's bytes (core/zoom zoom_f4_decode: decoders that work as the chip's, stopped at the block's end); past it ours writes nothing, where before stage 3's sweep of every command it wrote over its own working RAM and could fault (measured, tests/equiv/gatelock.py: an F4 on a sprite stream faulted the image). Live RAM, not ROM bytes: the player's ROM cannot supply them (the kind of B48 / B52 / B53). Measured: every F4 the game posts in the four rig corpora (29 posts, 4 sources, all 0x80) decodes to exactly 2,048 B, inside the block; so the stop is never reached in play.

entries.name: a sprite DMA list the 68000 never clears: past the register page $1FE0 the cart chip writes its descriptors on through its FPGA window; ours stores none there

scope.commands: AF (the frame end's first and second DMA descriptor) and AD (the composer's block-load descriptors) when the descriptor number $1F16 is 190 or more, so that its 16 bytes would not fit below $1FE0
scope.chip_ram: whatever the chip's stores to 0x68060000 + 0x1400 + 16 n (n >= 190) reach through its FPGA window

entries.rule: The chip lists each DMA descriptor at cart RAM $1400 + 16 n, n = $1F16, and the game clears $1F10 / $1F16 after its VBlank DMA, so a frame lists at most 17 (the composer's 15 loads, AF's two; verified). A list nobody clears grows on: from n = 177 the descriptors cover $1F10-$1F1F themselves (on the chip and here alike, so $1F16 takes a descriptor word), and from n = 190 they would reach the register page $1FE0-$1FFF and past cart RAM, which the chip writes through its FPGA window (0x68060000 + the offset; what the cart's FPGA does with such writes is not known) and where ours faulted on an unmapped store (measured, tests/equiv/gatelock.py with --no-clear before this row: post-C6 form 771, AF00, in spr_af_close). Ours now stores no descriptor that does not fit below $1FE0 (core/sprite SPR_DMA_FITS); the counts $1F10 / $1F16, the load list and the stash stay the chip's. The stage-1 images, which no hardware test build carries, are unchanged. Unreachable in play: the four test corpora's runs never come near (no fault, measured) and the game clears the list every frame.

entries.name: AA58, the MegaWire menu's restart: the cart chip restarts its MegaWire code inside the command and saves the MegaWire record to the EEPROM's slot 9; ours restarts it at the MegaWire task's next run and saves no record
entries.stage: 3+ (the images that run our MegaWire port from the SRAM image)

scope.commands: AA58 on mailbox B, the only AA form the chip accepts (no argument flag, low byte 0x58), and the forms whose state follows it
scope.save: the EEPROM's slot 9, its two 96-byte copies at 0xA00 and 0xA80: the record the chip's save (0x080215C0) writes there and ours does not
scope.timing: when the MegaWire reset (0x0802171C) and start-up (0x080218FC) run: inside the command on the chip, at the MegaWire task's next run on ours, up to about 0.1 s later

entries.rule: The cart chip's AA58 body (0x0801CCD0) calls the MegaWire reset 0x0802171C, which first saves the MegaWire record to the EEPROM's slot 9 (0x080215C0), then the MegaWire start-up 0x080218FC, both inside its mailbox interrupt. Ours accepts AA58 with the chip's gate and runs the reset and the start-up at the MegaWire task's next run, in the thread, because the start-up writes about 12.8 KB of SRAM, far more than a mailbox reply may take; the record save is not built. Measured on 2026-10-31 with tests/equiv/gatelock.py (aligned sampling) on the images with the MegaWire code merged: before and after C6 the AA58 form differs from the chip only in the save bytes of slot 9 that the chip writes (82 bytes); the forms after it are equal. The game posts AA58 only from its MegaWire menu, which needs a module plugged into the cart; the Pocket never has one, so the game never posts it there.
